QF.id: VIII Introduction to Forwards and Futures_67

question.text: An index is at 18,000. Futures with 120 days to expiry are trading at Rs. 18,400. Using continuous compounding with r = 9% and q = 1.5%, what can a trader conclude about the futures pricing?

answer.text: Futures are overpriced relative to fair value, creating a potential cash-and-carry arbitrage opportunity
Futures are underpriced relative to fair value (about Rs. 18,449.35), creating a potential reverse cash-and-carry arbitrage opportunity
Futures are fairly priced because the difference is within acceptable limits
No conclusion can be drawn because continuous compounding is not used in Indian markets

explanation.text: The Logic: Step-by-step analysis: 1. Fair value = S x e^((r - q) x T) = 18,000 x e^((0.09 - 0.015) x 120/365) = 18,000 x e^(0.02466) ≈ Rs. 18,449.35 2. Market futures price = Rs. 18,400 3. Since 18,400 < 18,449.35, futures are underpriced by about Rs. 49 Strategy: Reverse cash-and-carry arbitrage - Short the underlying at 18,000 (spot) and invest proceeds at r - Buy the underpriced futures at 18,400 - Lock in an arbitrage profit from the mispricing The Trap: Underpriced futures call for reverse cash-and-carry (short spot, buy futures), not cash-and-carry. The Rs. 100 gap between 18,400 and 18,300 in earlier versions of this item came from an incorrect fair value; recomputed correctly, the actual gap is about Rs. 49 the other way. Note: Pages 45 and 56 of the Series VIII workbook support continuous-compounding fair-value pricing; pages 44 and 94 state that futures below fair value imply reverse cash-and-carry while futures above fair value imply cash-and-carry.
